 Judgment

Dated this the 06th day of March, 2025 This Land Acquisition Appeal is filed by the State challenging the judgment and decree dated 11.02.2011 in L.A.R.No.61 of 2006 of the Subordinate Judge's Court, Pathanamthitta.
2.
An extent of 1.10 Ares of land comprised in Sy.No.355/29 and 0.95 Ares of land in Sy.No.355/30 of Kulanada Village in Kozhencherry Taluk were acquired for the purpose of widening the M.C.Road.
Section 4(1) notification was published on 05.06.2004.
The Land Acquisition Officer rendered an award dated 28.03.2005 and compensation of Rs.54,475/- per Are was awarded.
The reference court re-fixed the land value at Rs.4,94,200/- per Are.
This appeal has been filed challenging the said enhancement granted by the reference court.
3. Heard Smt.Rekha C.Nair, learned Senior Government Pleader for the appellants.
Though service of notice was completed on the respondent, there was no appearance on his behalf.
4. The learned Senior Government Pleader submitted that the reference court erred in enhancing the compensation and fixing 2025:KER:19518 it at Rs.2,00,000/- per cent.

The court ought to have considered that in L.A.R.No.31 of 2006 for a similar property, the 4(1) notification of which was just ten months prior to the 4(1) notification in this case, the award was for Rs.2,00,000/- per Are whereas in this case the award is for Rs.2,00,000/- per cent.
It is contended that the court below without any evidence took purported judicial notice that the land price had increased to Rs.2,00,000/- per cent in 2004 from Rs.1,36,364/- in the year 1995.
It is contended that at any rate Ext.A3 document which was relied on by the reference court was not a comparable document for fixing the land value.
It is submitted that the reference court had got carried away by the statement of AW1 that the acquired property is situated near Kulanada town.
It is also contended that Ext.A3 document and the property thereof are not discussed in the judgment.
Accordingly, it is contended that the reference court erred in fixing the enhanced value at Rs.4,94,000/- per Are i.e., at the rate of Rs.2,00,000/- per cent.

5. There is merit in the contention put forth by the learned Government Pleader that the reference court had fixed the land value at the rate of Rs.2,00,000/- per cent merely relying on Ext.A3 2025:KER:19518 which is of the year 1995 and by a skewed consideration of the escalation of land value till the year 2004.

It is submitted that for the very same purpose ten months prior to the 4 (1)
notification in this appeal, there was another acquisition, the 4(1) notification of which was on 08.08.2003.
The said acquisition was also in the same village and near Kulanada town.

Relying on the very same Ext.A3 sale deed, the reference court had awarded the enhanced compensation which was at the rate of Rs.2,00,000/- per Are whereas just after ten months of the 4(1) notification in this case the reference court awarded Rs.2,00,000/- per cent.
It is relevant to note that the reliance was on the very same document.

The said reference case was L.A.R.No.31 of 2006 of the Sub Court,
Pathanamthitta and the said judgment dated 29.11.2008 has become final.
It is very difficult to assume that the land value has increased 2 times within a shot span of ten months.
Therefore, the award of the court below is liable to be set aside.

sentences.text: It is noted that the judgment dated 29.11.2008 had been rendered by the same Sub Court in L.A.R.No.31 of 2006 with respect to a land situated near Kulanada town.

Section 4 (1)
2025:KER:19518 notification therein is dated 08.08.2003 which is nearly 10 months prior to the notification in the case at hand which was on 05.06.2004.

In the said L.A.R., taking note of the very same Ext.A3 sale deed dated 15.05.1995, wherein the land value was Rs.1,36,364/- per cent, the land value was fixed by the Court at Rs.2,00,000/- per Are equivalent to Rs.80,939/- per cent (1 Are =
2.471 cents).
However, in this reference under appeal, the Court had refixed the land value at Rs.4,94,200/- per Are @ 2,00,000/- per cent.

. This quantum jump in land value from Rs.2,00,000/- per Are to Rs.4,94,200/- per Are within a brief period of 10 months between the notification dates, is unreasonable and an anomaly which calls for correction.

It is even more so since it is the very same sale deed dated 15.05.1995 that is relied on in both references so to reach the widely varying conclusion of Rs.2,00,000/- per Are in the former and Rs.2,00,000/- per cent in the reference at hand.
The error apparent is thus very evident and glaring.

Though it could be surmised that the reference Court could have intended to apply the same land value @
Rs.2,00,000/- per Are to the case at hand too, such a supposition would lead to a 2025:KER:19518 substantial reduction in the land value of the acquired land of the claimant to Rs.80,939/- per cent from Rs.2,00,000/- per cent.

Moreover, the same would be an exercise that fails to take note of the ten-month difference in the dates of respective notifications under Section 4 (1) of the Act, which in effect accrues in favour of the claimant.

Thus it is evident from the dearth of legally reliable materials, retaining Ext.A3 as the best exemplar available, a certain amount of 'guesstimation' will have to be indulged in so as to arrive at a reasonable land value.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court has in New Okhla Industrial Development Authority v. Harnand Singh (Deceased) through LRs and others [(2024) SCC OnLine SC 1691] considered the applicability and use of the principle of 'guesstimation'
and has held that "32.

entities.text: New Okhla Industrial Development Authority v. Harnand Singh (Deceased) through LRs and others [(2024) SCC OnLine SC 1691]

sentences.text: This principle accentuates the fundamental understanding that determining compensation for land is not a matter of exact science but involves a significant element of estimation.
Indeed, this holds true for valuation of land in general, which is affected by a multitude of factors such as its location, surrounding market conditions, feasible uses etc.
Accordingly, while evidence and calculations can aid in estimating the land value, they ultimately serve as tools for approximation rather than precision.

Instead, land valuation--and consequently the affixation of compensation remains an exercise of informed estimation, requiring the integration of diverse data points and professional judgment concerning subjective, intangible and dynamic elements.
Pursuing a single precise valuation or compensation figure is bound to be unjust, representing a rigid approach and a 2025:KER:19518 procrustean endeavour at best.
33. Having said that, it is important to clarify that the process of determining compensation is not entirely subjective.
While it may not be possible to arrive at a definitive figure, the exercise is still epistemologically objective in so far as it is grounded in evidence and the consideration of relevant factors.

In case the compensation is fixed agnostically to the factors affecting the valuation of the land, the resultant figure might be arbitrary and may fail to adequately compensate the landowner for the expropriated land.
Hence, while some subjectivity may exist in fixing the final figure based on these factors, the sliding scale of judicial discretion cannot be extended to mere speculation.
34. Accordingly, while the Court can use the principle of guesstimation in reasonably estimating the value of land in the absence of direct evidence, the exercise ought not to be purely hypothetical.

sentences.text: Instead, the Court must embrace a holistic view and consider all relevant factors and existing evidence, even if not directly comparable, to arrive at a fair determination of compensation."
(Emphasis added)

The Hon'ble Supreme Court has laid down the three categories of relevant factors that ought to be considered while determining the estimated value of the land to determine a fair amount of compensation in land acquisition proceedings.

The same are as follows:
"i. Characteristics of the land: The valuation of land is undeniably influenced by its inherent characteristics.

A parcel of land endowed with advantageous features that enhance its accessibility and usability tends to command higher market price and thus, a greater valuation in comparison to lands lacking such attributes.

Key factors contributing to such features include connectivity via roads and other means of transportation, the size and shape of the land, availability of essential utilities such as electricity and water, the evenness or levelling of the land's surface, width of 2025:KER:19518 frontage, and nature and status of the surrounding area etc.

ii. 
Future potentiality of the land:
In addition to its characteristics, the valuation of land is also influenced by its potentiality.

Lands with the potential to be used for commercial or residential purposes; that are located in or near a developed area; or which are proximate to tourist destinations, are perceived to hold greater value in the future.
Consequently, landowners may anticipate higher future prices and accordingly demand higher sale prices compared to lands lacking these attributes.
Accordingly, these features also lead to an increase in valuation; and iii. Factors denoting market sentiment:
Market sentiments are powerful drivers of land valuation.

Even if a particular piece of land possesses all desirable features, its valuation can still suffer if the market conditions at the time of publication of the notification under Section 4 of the 1894 Act were unfavourable.
Factors such as economic recessions, political instability, speculative investments or real estate crisis can impact the perceived value of the land.

Thus, these extraneous economic and political factors must also be considered when assessing land valuation."(Emphasis added)
7.

Bearing in mind the above mandate as laid down by the Supreme Court, and after factoring in the lack of reliable independent evidence to show that the acquired property is similarly situated as the property covered vide Ext.A3 sale deed, it is deemed fit and reasonable that an amount of Rs.1,15,000/- per cent ie., Rs.2,84,165/-
per Are be fixed as the land value for the acquired land.
Thus the land value of the acquired land is re
- fixed at Rs.2,84,165/- per Are instead of Rs.4,94,200/- per Are as arrived at by the reference court.
The L.A.A. is allowed to the above extent.

The land value awarded in judgment and decree dated 11.02.2011 in L.A.R.No. 61 of 2006 of the Subordinate Judge's Court,
Pathanamthitta, shall stand modified as Rs.1,15,000/- per cent ie., Rs.2,84,165/- per Are.

The L.A.A. is disposed of as above.
